newsitem.title: GERMANY: German employers chief denies backdown on sick pay.
newsitem.headline: German employers chief denies backdown on sick pay.

text.p: Werner Stumpfe, chairman of the German metal employers assocation, denied on Monday that an agreement struck with the IG Metall trade union represented a back-down from its previous position on sick pay cuts.
"Today's statement is completely neutral for both sides," Stumpfe said after a news conference that followed the talks, held at a hotel near Frankfurt.

Asked whether Gesamtmetall, which had earlier recommended that its members apply a new law on sick cuts immediately, was now being less aggressive in its stance, Stumpfe replied, "We have never adopted an aggressive stance.
"It was IG Metall that acted aggressively with walkouts leading to millions of marks of costs," he added.

"Every time we have tried to cut labour costs we have met with the fiercest resistance of the unions," Stumpfe said, adding that it was was not for the unions to decide whether such a move by a company constituted breach of contract.

The two sides have been at loggerheads over a new law empowering employers to cut sick pay to 80 percent of the standard pay rate. Previously, employees absent through illness had been paid at full rates.

At the end of Monday's talks, the employers agreed to recommend that companies take no action to cut sick pay for the time being in return for an IG Metall reassurance that its walk-outs and protests will be suspended.

Several major companies had taken advantage of the new law to cut sick pay rates immediately, even though politicians from Chancellor Helmut Kohl down had recommended that the law should not be implemented until new wgae contracts were negotiated.
Some companies, including Daimler Benz AG and Ford reversed their announcements, saying they would temporarily reinstate full sick pay, after the outcome of today's talks became known.
